question:
A previously healthy 21-year-old man reports a one-week history of easy bruising and bleeding from
the gums when flossing his teeth. He has no other personal or family history of bleeding. He takes no
medications and does not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. He seems somewhat anxious during the
interview. His vital signs are normal. Examination of the oropharynx reveals blood around the gums
and a few hemorrhagic bullous lesions on the mucosa. His skin shows numerous petechiae. There is
no lymphadenopathy. The liver and spleen are not palpable. Laboratory testing reveals a platelet count
of 10,000 per mm3 (reference range, 150,000–350,000), a hemoglobin level of 14 g/dL (13.5–17.5)
with normal indices, and a leukocyte count of 7500 per mm3 (4500–11,000) with normal differential. A
peripheral blood smear shows decreased platelets, which are well granulated and larger than normal.
Leukocyte and erythrocyte morphology are normal without any schistocytes. The serum lactate
dehydrogenase, prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, and fibrinogen levels are
normal. Hepatitis C virus and HIV tests are negative. Which one of the following next steps is most
appropriate for this patient? Answer Choices: (A) Administer intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) (B)
Start platelet transfusion (C) Perform bone marrow biopsy (D) Initiate dexamethasone therapy (E) Test
for platelet glycoprotein autoantibodies (F) Measure ADAMTS13 level (G) Screen for von Willebrand
disease (H) Test for antiphospholipid antibodies (I) Order a direct Coombs test (J) Perform splenic
ultrasound
 A. Start platelet transfusion

B. Perform splenic ultrasound
